learningObjective: Reason about the peak activation memory of standard attention backward and how FlashAttention-style recomputation changes it.

canonicalClaims.claim: Naive attention backward keeps the [B, H, N, N] softmax matrix P (or logits S) as an activation for use in gradient formulas; this quadratic-in-N tensor dominates activation memory and limits training context length.
conditions: Standard autograd-derived backward without I/O-aware fusion.
P is materialized in HBM (as in most default frameworks pre-FA).
nonImplications: Does not imply P must always be stored; FA shows an alternative.

canonicalClaims.claim: FlashAttention backward stores only per-row (m, l) statistics (O(B*H*N)) from forward and recomputes P block-by-block in backward using Q, K, and dO; total FLOPs increase (extra recomputation), but HBM I/O drops sharply, giving wall-clock speedup.
conditions: SMEM per SM large enough for a Q/K/V tile.
nonImplications: Does not imply FA backward matches naive FLOP count.
Does not imply recomputation is always the right choice; short-sequence workloads may prefer storing P.

misconceptions.claim: The full P matrix must be HBM-resident at some point in any correct attention backward.
misconceptions.whyWrong: FlashAttention shows a tiled backward that avoids full-P materialization.

misconceptions.claim: FA backward has the same total FLOPs as naive backward.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Backward recomputes P, adding FLOPs; the trade is I/O for compute.

misconceptions.claim: Attention backward memory is linear in N.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Naive backward is quadratic in N due to storing P; FA collapses this to linear.

implementationFacts: FA stores l_i = sum exp(x - m_i) and m_i per row; combined size is O(B*H*N).
Some frameworks offer 'attention with checkpoint' as a middle ground: store P but no dP intermediate.
performanceScenarios: Long-context training (>8K tokens) is essentially only tractable with FA-style backward.
Even short-sequence training benefits marginally from FA due to reduced HBM I/O.
